question: What does a linear search do?
correct: Checks the items one at a time from the front until it finds the target
incorrect: Jumps to the middle item and throws away the half without the target
Sorts the list first and then reads off the item in the first position
Checks the first item and the last item, then works in toward the middle
feedback: Linear search is the plain one: start at the front and look at each item in turn. It needs nothing from the list — no ordering, no preparation — which is why it is the only choice when the data is unsorted.

question: Arrange these lines into a working linear search that returns the position of the target, or None when it is not there.
feedback: The final return sits OUTSIDE the loop, at the same indentation as the for. Pull it inside and the function gives up after checking only the first item — the single most common bug in a hand-written search.

question: Trace this linear search. What does the program print?
feedback: The search returns the moment it meets a match, so it reports index 1 and never looks at the second 9. A linear search finds the FIRST match.

question: In our search functions, what value signals 'not found'?
correct: None, Python's built-in 'nothing here' value
incorrect: -1, the way many other programming languages do it
0, since it is the first list index
An empty list with no items in it
feedback: We return None as the sentinel for 'not found'. Avoid -1 in Python, because -1 is a valid index meaning the last item.

question: This search has a bug: its final return has slipped inside the loop. What does the program print?
correct: None
feedback: On the very first pass items[0] is 4, which is not the target, so the else runs and the function returns None — having looked at one item. "Not found" can only be decided AFTER the loop has checked everything, which is why that return belongs outside the loop.

question: A special return value meaning "not found", such as the None these search functions return, is called a ___ value.
correct: sentinel
feedback: A sentinel is a value chosen to signal a condition rather than to be real data. Choosing a safe one matters: -1 is a poor sentinel in Python because it is also a valid index.

question: A linear search checks items from the front, one at a time. The target sits at index {{p}} of a list of {{n}} items. How many items has the search checked when it returns?
feedback_template: Indexes start at 0, so index {{p}} is item number {{expected}}: the search checks {{expected}} items and stops. The rest of the {{n}} are never looked at.

question: NPC: Halving the shelf
intro: The library runs deeper than the torchlight reaches. Nia rests a hand on a shelf of numbered ledgers. “Fifteen ledgers, already in order. A slow apprentice starts at the left. Watch what a fast one does.”

steps.say: I want ledger 23 — call it the target. I don't touch the first ledger — I go straight to the MIDDLE one. It reads 20. Since 23 is bigger than 20, and the shelf is sorted, every ledger from the middle leftwards is out. Eight ledgers eliminated by looking at one.

beats.say: I want ledger 23 — call it the target. I don't touch the first ledger — I go straight to the MIDDLE one. It reads 20.
Since 23 is bigger than 20, and the shelf is sorted, every ledger from the middle leftwards is out. Eight ledgers eliminated by looking at one.

steps.say: Seven remain, to the right of where I looked.

check.answer: The middle of the seven that remain
wrong: The first of the seven that remain
The last ledger on the whole shelf
check.why: Every pass repeats the same move on whatever is left — that is what makes it halve so fast.

steps.say: The counts go 15, then 7, then 3, then 1. Four looks at worst. Double the shelf to 31 and it costs just ONE more look — that is what O(log n) means. This halving search is called binary search, and all of it depends on the shelf being sorted; on an unsorted shelf the trick is worthless.

beats.say: The counts go 15, then 7, then 3, then 1. Four looks at worst. Double the shelf to 31 and it costs just ONE more look — that is what O(log n) means.
This halving search is called binary search. All of it depends on the shelf being sorted; on an unsorted shelf the trick is worthless.

outro: “Now a shelf of your own. Count the looks.”

question: A sorted list has {{n}} items. At most how many items does a binary search have to look at before it has either found the target or run out of list?
feedback_template: Each look halves what is left, so the count is how many times {{n}} can be halved down to nothing: floor(log2 {{n}}) + 1 = {{expected}} looks.

question: Arrange the moves of one pass of binary search over a sorted list.
items: Look at the item in the middle of the range still in play
Compare that item with the target
Discard the half that cannot contain the target
Repeat on the half that remains
feedback: Each pass looks at the middle, compares, throws away the half the target cannot be in, and repeats on the rest — which is why the work grows only logarithmically.

question: A student runs a correct binary search function on a list that was never sorted. What is the most likely result?
correct: It may report the target as missing, because it throws away the wrong half
incorrect: It still finds the target, but takes O(n) time rather than O(log n) time
Python raises an error, since binary search checks the ordering as it goes
It finds the target but hands back the position of a neighbouring item
feedback: Binary search decides which half to keep by assuming everything left of the middle is smaller. With no ordering, that assumption is simply false, and the half holding the target can be discarded on the very first comparison. Nothing in the code detects the problem, so the wrong answer comes back quietly.

question: A search that repeatedly halves a sorted list to find a target is called a ___ search.
correct: binary
feedback: Binary search halves the remaining items each step, giving O(log n) running time on sorted data.

question: NPC: Keeping track of low, mid and high
intro: Nia writes seven sorted numbers on the slate. “The shelf trick works on any sorted list. In code, the range still in play is held by two numbers.”

steps.say: low and high are the positions of the two ends of the range still in play. mid is the position halfway between them. I am searching for the target 40, and items[3] is 20.

beats.say: low and high are the positions of the two ends of the range still in play. mid is the position halfway between them.
I am searching for the target 40, and items[3] is 20.

steps.say: 20 is smaller than the target, so the target cannot be at mid or anywhere to its left. I move low to mid + 1.

check.prompt: low becomes 4 and high stays 6. Which position is the new mid?
wrong: 4, the first position still in play
6, the last position still in play
check.why: mid is worked out fresh from the current low and high on every pass.

steps.say: items[5] is 40 — the target, after two looks: 20, then 40. If low ever passes high, the range is empty and the function returns None: not found.

outro: “Trace the next one yourself. Write down every item the search looks at.”

question: This binary search records every item it looks at. What does the program print?
code:
items = [4, 7, 10, 15, 22, 28, 35]
target = 22
low, high = 0, len(items) - 1
seen = []
while low <= high:
    mid = (low + high) // 2
    seen.append(items[mid])
    if items[mid] == target:
        break
    elif items[mid] < target:
        low = mid + 1
    else:
        high = mid - 1
print(seen)
feedback: low and high start at 0 and 6, so the first look is index 3 (15). 22 is bigger, so low becomes 4 and the next look is index 5 (28). 22 is smaller, so high becomes 4, and the last look is index 4 — the target.

prompt: Fill in the blanks to finish this binary search over a sorted list.
feedback: Integer division keeps mid a whole number, which a list index has to be. Each end then moves PAST mid — to mid + 1 or mid - 1 — because mid itself has just been checked. Moving an end only to mid is what makes a binary search loop forever on a missing value.

question: The target is not in the list. What does the program print?
code:
items = [4, 7, 10, 15, 22, 28, 35]
target = 8
low, high = 0, len(items) - 1
looks = 0
while low <= high:
    mid = (low + high) // 2
    looks = looks + 1
    if items[mid] == target:
        break
    elif items[mid] < target:
        low = mid + 1
    else:
        high = mid - 1
print(looks, low > high)
correct: 3 True
feedback: The search looks at 15, then 7, then 10, and each time moves an end past mid. After the third look low has passed high: the range is empty, the loop ends, and a search function would return None.

question: Which Big-O describes linear search, and which describes binary search?
correct: Linear search is O(n); binary search is O(log n)
incorrect: Linear search is O(log n); binary search is O(n)
Both are O(n), but binary search has a smaller constant
Linear search is O(1); binary search is O(n log n)
feedback: Doubling the list doubles linear search's worst case, but adds only one step to binary search. Among a billion items, linear search may check a billion and binary search checks about 30.

question: Doubling the size of a list roughly doubles the work of a {{1}} search, but adds only one extra step to a {{2}} search — which pays for that speed by requiring the list to be {{3}} before you start.
feedback: O(n) work scales in step with the list, while O(log n) work grows by one step per doubling. Halving only works when order tells you which half to throw away, so binary search buys its speed with a precondition linear search does not need.

question: You need to search a large collection many times, and you are free to prepare it first. Which approach is best?
correct: Sort it once, then use binary search for every lookup
incorrect: Use linear search each time and skip the sorting cost
Sort it once, then use linear search for every lookup
Use binary search straight away, since sorting is optional
feedback: Sorting is a one-time cost that makes every later search logarithmic. When you search a lot, that trade pays for itself quickly; for a single lookup on unsorted data, plain linear search is simpler.

question: Match each Big-O class to a description of how its work grows.

pairs.definition: Constant: the same work for any input size
Grows slowly, like repeatedly halving the data
Grows in direct proportion to the input
Grows with the square of the input

feedback: These classes rank how fast work grows: constant, logarithmic, linear, and quadratic, from most to least scalable.

question: Arrange these growth rates from slowest-growing to fastest-growing as n gets large.
feedback: Constant work never grows; logarithmic barely does; linear keeps pace with the input; n log n is a little worse, which is why merge sort beats selection sort; and quadratic climbs sharply, doubling the input roughly quadrupling the work.

question: An O(n squared) algorithm takes {{t}} milliseconds on a list of {{n}} items. About how many milliseconds should it take on {{k}} times as many items?
feedback_template: Squared growth means multiplying the input by {{k}} multiplies the work by {{k}} x {{k}}, so {{t}} ms becomes about {{expected}} ms. The input grew {{k}} times, but the cost grew far more.

question: NPC: One pass of selection sort
intro: Nia lays five numbered tiles face-up: 5, 3, 9, 1, 6. “Selection sort is the one people mis-describe. It does not shuffle things along. It picks, and it swaps. One pass.”

steps.say: The sorted part grows from the front. Pass one, so position 0 is the slot I am filling. To fill it I scan the WHOLE row for the smallest tile. Scanning 5, 3, 9, 1, 6 — the smallest is 1, sitting in position 3.

beats.say: The sorted part grows from the front. Pass one, so position 0 is the slot I am filling. To fill it I scan the WHOLE row for the smallest tile.
Scanning 5, 3, 9, 1, 6 — the smallest is 1, sitting in position 3.

steps.say: Now the move that people get wrong.

check.prompt: The smallest tile is 1, at position 3. How does it reach position 0?
check.answer: It swaps places with the tile currently in position 0
wrong: Everything between them shifts right to make room
It is removed and appended to the end
check.why: Selection sort swaps just those two tiles. Nothing else moves — that is what makes one pass cheap.

steps.say: So 1 and 5 trade places and the row reads 1, 3, 9, 5, 6. Note that 5 landed where 1 used to be, and 3, 9, 6 never moved. Position 0 is finished forever; pass two scans only the unsorted tail — everything after it.

outro: “Same move, different tiles, next question. Scan for the smallest, then swap it to the front.”

question: Given  ranks = [7, 2, 10, 4, 1], what does the list look like after the FIRST pass of selection sort?
feedback: The first pass finds the smallest item (1, at the end) and swaps it with whatever was in slot 0. The 7 that was displaced lands where the 1 had been; nothing shifts along, and only one slot is finished after one pass.

question: How does selection sort work?
correct: Find the smallest remaining item, swap it into place, and repeat
incorrect: Split the list in half repeatedly, then merge the sorted halves
Compare neighboring pairs and swap them until no swaps remain
Insert each item into a second list at the right position
feedback: The outer loop walks the slot being filled and the inner loop scans the unsorted tail for the smallest item. After each pass, the sorted front of the list grows by one.

question: This is one pass of selection sort, written out. What does the program print?
code:
nums = [6, 9, 2, 7]
smallest = 0
for i in range(1, len(nums)):
    if nums[i] < nums[smallest]:
        smallest = i
nums[0], nums[smallest] = nums[smallest], nums[0]
print(nums[0], nums[2])
feedback: The loop leaves smallest holding index 2, where the 2 is. The swap then trades slot 0 with slot 2, so the 2 comes to the front and the 6 it displaced lands where the 2 was.

question: Write the one-line Python statement that swaps the values of two variables a and b.
correct: a, b = b, a
b, a = a, b
feedback: a, b = b, a swaps the two values in a single statement using tuple unpacking.

question: Selection sort scans the whole unsorted tail on every pass, and there is one pass per item. Which Big-O class does that give it?
correct: O(n²), because roughly n passes each do work proportional to n
incorrect: O(n), because each item is placed exactly once into its final slot
O(n log n), because the unsorted tail halves on each pass
O(log n), because only the smallest item is examined each time
feedback: Roughly n passes, each scanning up to n items, multiplies out to n². Doubling the list therefore roughly quadruples the work.

question: Selection sort on a list of {{n}} items makes {{n}} - 1 comparisons on its first pass, {{n}} - 2 on the next, and so on down to 1. How many comparisons is that altogether?
feedback_template: Adding {{n}}-1 + {{n}}-2 + ... + 1 gives {{n}} x ({{n}} - 1) / 2 = {{expected}} comparisons. That total grows with the square of {{n}}, which is why selection sort is O(n squared).

question: Merge sort uses divide and conquer. Which description matches it?
correct: Split until each pile is one item, then merge sorted piles upward
incorrect: Scan for the smallest item, place it, and repeat on the rest
Sort the first half completely, then append the second half unsorted
Compare the first and last items and work inwards to the middle
feedback: A single item is already sorted, and merging two sorted piles is cheap. There are about log n levels of splitting, each doing O(n) merging work, which is where O(n log n) comes from.

question: Merge sort splits a list in half over and over until every pile holds a single item. Starting from {{n}} items, how many rounds of splitting does that take?
feedback_template: Each round halves the pile size, so the number of rounds is log2({{n}}) = {{expected}}. Those {{expected}} levels, each costing about n work to merge, are where the n log n in merge sort comes from.

question: Why is merge sort usually preferred over selection sort for large lists?
correct: Its work grows far more slowly as the list gets longer
incorrect: It sorts in place, while selection sort needs a second list
It makes a single pass, while selection sort makes about n
It copes with unsorted input, which selection sort cannot
feedback: Merge sort is O(n log n) and selection sort is O(n²). On ten items nobody could tell them apart; on a million, one finishes in a blink and the other is still running. (It is selection sort that works in place — merge sort pays for its speed with extra memory.)

question: Match each algorithm to its typical Big-O running time.

pairs.definition: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n²)
O(n log n)

feedback: Knowing an algorithm's Big-O lets you predict how it will scale before you ever run it on large data.

question: Which of these are true about  sorted(items)  and  items.sort()? (Select all that apply)
correct: sorted(items) returns a new list and leaves the original alone
items.sort() rearranges the original list and returns None
incorrect: Both leave the original list unchanged
sorted(items) only works on lists of numbers
items.sort() must be given a key function to work
feedback: Writing x = mylist.sort() and getting None back is a classic beginner bug. Use sorted() when you want a new list, and .sort() when you mean to rearrange the original in place.

question: A list is sorted with its .sort() method. What does this program print?
correct: None
feedback: .sort() rearranges a itself and hands nothing back, so b is None. The sorted data is in a — writing b = a.sort() is how a correct sort appears to "lose" a list.

question: A list is sorted with the sorted() function. What does this program print?
feedback: sorted() builds a NEW list and leaves a exactly as it was, so a still starts with 3 while b starts with 1.

prompt: Fill in the blanks so this sorts the list in place and then prints the smallest score.
question:
scores = [5, 2, 9]
scores.{{1}}()
print(scores[{{2}}])
feedback: The in-place method is called on the list and changes it directly, so scores itself is now in order and the smallest value sits at index 0. Writing scores = scores.sort() would replace the list with None.

question: Rearranging a list without making a new copy is described as sorting ___ (two words joined by a hyphen).
correct: in-place
in place
feedback: An in-place sort like nums.sort() rearranges the existing list rather than building a new one.

question: NPC: Telling sorted() what to compare
intro: Nia sets down three name-cards, each with a score chalked on the back. “sorted() can order numbers and words by itself. Hand it dictionaries and it has no idea which part you care about — so you tell it.”

steps.say: A key function takes ONE item and returns the value to sort by. Here each item is a student dictionary, and the function returns that student's score.

beats.say: A key function takes ONE item and returns the value to sort by.
Here each item is a student dictionary, and the function returns that student's score.

steps.say: I pass the function itself to sorted() — its name, with no parentheses. sorted() calls it once for every item and orders the items by what comes back.

beats.say: I pass the function itself to sorted() — its name, with no parentheses.
sorted() calls it once for every item and orders the items by what comes back.

check.prompt: Why is it key=by_score and not key=by_score()?
check.answer: sorted() needs the function itself, to call on each item
wrong: The parentheses are optional, so either spelling works
With parentheses it would sort the list in place instead
check.why: by_score() would call it right now, with no student to look at. key= wants the function, to call later.

steps.say: The smallest key comes first. Add reverse=True for largest first. Items whose keys are equal keep the order they started in.

outro: “Your turn. Work out each item's key before you decide the order.”

question: This sorts three words with a key function. What does the program print?
code:
def last(word):
    return word[-1]

words = ["cab", "bee", "ada"]
print(sorted(words, key=last)[0])
correct: ada
feedback: The keys are the last letters: b for cab, e for bee, a for ada. Ordered by those keys the list is ada, cab, bee — so index 0 is ada. The words themselves are never compared.

question: A list of student dictionaries, each holding a 'score' key, must be listed from the highest score down to the lowest. Which approach does that?
correct: Call sorted() with a key that returns the score and reverse set to True
incorrect: Call sorted() with a key that returns the score, which lists them highest first
Call sorted() with no key at all, since it compares the score values by itself
Call .sort() with reverse set to True and assign the list it returns to a name
feedback: A key function tells sorted() what to compare, but the default direction is still ascending, so descending order needs reverse=True as well. sorted() cannot guess which field of a dictionary matters, and .sort() rearranges the list in place and returns None, so assigning its result throws the data away.

prompt: Fill in the blanks so this prints the words ordered shortest to longest, leaving the original list untouched.
question:
words = ["pear", "fig", "banana"]
ordered = {{1}}(words, key={{2}})
print(ordered)
feedback: sorted() returns a new list, which is what lets the original survive; words.sort() would rearrange it in place and return None. The key is passed as a function, without parentheses — Python calls it once per item to decide what to compare.

question: Match each Python sorting call to what it produces, assuming nums is a list of numbers and words is a list of strings.

pairs.definition: A new list running smallest to largest, with nums left untouched
Nothing returned at all — nums itself is rearranged in place
A new list running largest to smallest
A new list of the same words ordered shortest to longest
One value: the largest number in the list

feedback: The sorted() family always hands back a new list and leaves the original alone, while .sort() does the opposite and returns None. A key function changes what gets compared, and reverse changes the direction — they are independent settings you can use together.

question: This line must sort the list in place from the largest value down to the smallest:  scores.sort(___)  Write just what goes inside the parentheses.
correct: reverse=True
feedback: In place means the .sort() method, called on the list itself; reverse=True turns the usual smallest-first order round. sorted(scores, reverse=True) would give the same order, but as a new list.

question: Match each technique to when you would reach for it.

pairs.definition: The data is unsorted or the list is tiny
The data is sorted and you search it often
Learning how sorting works, or a very small list
Real code, where a fast built-in sort is wanted

feedback: In practice you almost never hand-write a sort. Knowing how they work is what lets you judge which tool fits and what it will cost.

question: What is a Turing machine?
correct: A thought experiment: a tape, a head that reads and writes, and a table of rules
incorrect: The first electronic computer, built to break codes during the Second World War
A test of whether a machine's written answers can pass for those of a person
A program that decides whether any other program will finish or run forever
feedback: Turing imagined the simplest machine that could still carry out any step-by-step procedure: a tape of symbols, a head that reads and writes one at a time, and a rulebook. Nobody builds one. Its use is as a definition — a precise way to say what "can be computed" means.

question: What does the Church-Turing thesis claim?
correct: Anything computable at all can be computed by a Turing machine
incorrect: Any program that halts can be made to run in reasonable time
Every problem has an algorithm if you look hard enough
Turing machines are faster than the computers we build today
feedback: This is why we can speak of computation as one universal idea rather than a different idea per machine. Your phone can compute no class of things that the tape-and-rulebook gadget could not.

question: What does the halting problem ask?
correct: Given any program and its input, will it finish or run forever?
incorrect: Given any program and its input, how many steps will it take?
Given any two programs, which of them will finish sooner?
Given any program that stopped, which line made it stop?
feedback: The halting problem asks for one program that can look at ANY other program, with its input, and say correctly whether it will ever stop. Turing proved that no such program can exist.

question: What does it mean to say the halting problem is undecidable?
correct: No algorithm can answer correctly in every case, whatever its resources
incorrect: The problem takes so long to solve that no computer has finished a run yet
The answer depends on which programming language is used
A correct algorithm exists, but nobody has managed to find it yet
feedback: Undecidable is not the same as hard. A hard problem can be solved slowly; an undecidable one has no correct general algorithm at all — faster hardware changes nothing.

question: Real tools such as antivirus scanners and infinite-loop detectors exist even though the underlying questions are undecidable. How is that possible?
correct: They settle for being usually right, or right on limited cases
incorrect: They run the program to completion first and then report the answer exactly
They rely on hardware that is not a Turing machine
They only work on programs written without any loops
feedback: Undecidability rules out a perfect general answer, not a useful partial one. Practical tools trade completeness for usefulness — which is why an antivirus can miss things and a type checker rejects some safe programs.

question: Match each term about the limits of computation to what it says.

pairs.definition: Some algorithm solves it, however slowly
No algorithm can be right in every case
An algorithm exists, but needs impractical time
Problems an algorithm can solve quickly
Problems whose proposed answers can be checked quickly

feedback: Three different questions are in play. Computable or undecidable asks whether an algorithm exists at all. Tractable or intractable asks whether it finishes in a useful time. P and NP sort the solvable problems by whether answers are quick to find or only quick to check.

question: Which pair of statements correctly describes the classes P and NP?
correct: P problems are solved quickly; NP answers can be checked quickly
incorrect: P answers can be checked quickly; NP problems are solved quickly
P problems have proven fast algorithms; NP problems have proven slow ones
P problems are decidable, while NP problems are undecidable
feedback: Assembling a thousand-piece jigsaw may be brutal, but glancing at a finished one to confirm it is right is quick. That gap between finding and checking is what P versus NP is about.

question: Why is the question "does P equal NP?" famous?
correct: Nobody has proved it either way, and a proof wins a million dollars
incorrect: It was proved false in 1936 and is now only of historical interest
It asks whether any computer can outperform a Turing machine
It determines how fast a sorting algorithm is allowed to be
feedback: Almost everyone believes finding is genuinely harder than checking, but belief is not proof. It is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, and much of modern encryption quietly depends on the answer being no.

question: A brute-force packing program tries every way of choosing which of {{n}} boxes to load. Each box is either in or out. How many combinations must it try?
feedback_template: Every box doubles the count, so {{n}} boxes give 2 to the power {{n}} = {{expected}} combinations. Ten more boxes would make it about a thousand times larger. That doubling is what makes a problem intractable: solvable in principle, hopeless at size.

question: A problem that can be solved in principle, but needs an impractical amount of work to solve, is called ___.
correct: intractable
feedback: Intractable sits between easy and impossible: the algorithm exists, but running it on a real input would take longer than anyone can wait.

question: Which of the following statements about the limits of computation are correct? (Select all that apply)
correct: The halting problem cannot be solved by any program, including AI
Some problems are solvable in principle but intractable in practice
Being easy to check does not guarantee a problem is easy to solve
incorrect: A fast enough computer could eventually solve the halting problem
Every problem in NP is already known to be in P
feedback: Undecidable problems like halting are impossible for any program, intractable problems are merely impractical, and whether NP equals P is unknown. No amount of speed crosses the undecidable wall.

question: Which of these are limits about cost rather than about impossibility? (Select all that apply)
correct: Finding the provably best packing for a truck full of oddly shaped boxes
Scheduling five hundred classes with no conflicts, guaranteed optimally
incorrect: Writing one program that decides whether any given program halts
Writing one checker that decides whether any two programs always agree
feedback: Packing and scheduling have answers that an algorithm can find; the trouble is that guaranteeing the best one may take impractically long, which makes them intractable. Deciding whether a program halts, or whether two programs always agree, is undecidable: no correct general algorithm exists at all.

question: Why can't a more powerful AI or LLM solve an undecidable problem like the halting problem?
correct: The limit is mathematical, so no program can cross it
incorrect: AI simply has not been trained on enough examples yet
AI runs on hardware that is currently too slow
AI learns from data, so proofs about algorithms miss it
feedback: Undecidability is a proven mathematical limit on algorithms themselves. An AI is still a program, so it is bound by the same wall, no matter how capable it becomes.

question: Return the index of the first item equal to target. If the target is not in the list, return None.
hint: Loop over the positions with `range(len(items))`. The `return None` belongs after the loop, not inside it.
feedback: Linear search: return as soon as a match appears, and only decide "not found" once the loop has checked every item. None is the sentinel — -1 would also be a valid index.

question: Return a new list holding the same words, ordered from shortest to longest. Words of equal length stay in their original order.
hint: `sorted()` takes a `key=` function that says what to compare. One built-in already measures a word.
feedback: key=len hands sorted() each word's length to compare instead of the word. Ties keep their original order, which is why bb still comes before cc.

question: Each student is a dictionary with a 'name' and a 'score'. Return a list of the names, ordered from the highest score to the lowest. Students with equal scores stay in their original order.
hint: Write a small `def` inside your answer that returns one student's score, and pass its name as `key=`. `reverse=True` puts the highest first.
feedback: A key function turns each dictionary into the one value worth comparing. sorted() hands back the whole dictionaries in the new order, so a loop then collects the names.

question: Return the INDEX of the smallest item found at position start or later. If the smallest value appears more than once, return the first of those positions.
hint: Keep the index of the best item so far, starting at `start`, and compare each later item against it.
feedback: This is the scan at the heart of selection sort: remember WHERE the smallest item is, not what it is, because the swap that follows needs a position. Using < rather than <= keeps the first of any ties.

question: Carry out exactly k passes of selection sort on the list and return it. One pass finds the smallest item in the unsorted tail and swaps it into the next slot from the front.
hint: An outer loop over the slot being filled, `for slot in range(k):`, with the smallest-item scan inside it and one swap after the scan.
feedback: Selection sort is two loops: the outer one walks the slot being filled, the inner one scans the unsorted tail for the smallest item, and a single swap finishes the pass. After k passes the first k slots are final and the rest are not sorted yet — which is why sorted() cannot answer this one.

question: A binary search keeps two positions, low and high, starting at the two ends of a sorted list. Each pass looks at the item at (low + high) // 2, and stops if it is the target; otherwise it moves low or high just past that position. Return how many items the search looks at, whether or not it finds the target.
hint: Write the binary search loop, add one to a counter each time you work out `mid`, and return the counter in both places the search can end.
feedback: Seven items never take more than three looks, found or not: that is O(log n) made visible. A linear search for 47 in the same list would look at all seven.
